proposals.definition: Guṇḍarīpāda, the siddha to whom the manuscript attributes song 4. He names himself Guḍarī in its last couplet; the manuscript also spells the name Guṇḍarī and Guḍḍarī, and the Tibetan translation guN+Da rI. Munidatta calls him a siddha master who has directly realized the vajra-like samādhi (cp.04.m6).
proposals.rationale: Poet of the song, named in the attribution, the last couplet and the commentary; the unit already refers to him as p-gundari, and the -pāda form follows the heading style (Lūyīpāda).

proposals.definition: The name of the rāga (melodic mode) to which song 4 is sung, given in its heading. The Tibetan translation calls the melody skya rengs, 'dawn', as if the name were Sanskrit aruṇa, 'dawn-red'; whether aru is a shortened form of that word is uncertain.
proposals.rationale: Rāga names in headings stay in source form, like Paṭamañjarī; this is the first occurrence of Aru in the text.

proposals.definition: A woman who practises yoga; in the yoginī tantras also a class of female deities, and the partner of the male adept. In song 4 the poet addresses a yoginī, asking for her embrace and saying he cannot live a moment without her. Munidatta identifies her with Nairātmā, the purified avadhūtikā (cp.04.m2).
proposals.symbolicImage: the yoginī whom the poet addresses and asks for an embrace

symbolicReadings.referent: Nairātmā, the selfless yoginī, who is the purified avadhūtikā once the three channels have been pressed and made free of appearance
Nairātmā, addressed as the yoginī without whom he cannot hold the vital wind for a moment
Nairātmā in the form of bodhicitta, who rises from the root of the jewel to the wheel of great bliss

proposals.rationale: The yoginī is addressed three times in the song and carries Munidatta's chief equation; without an entry জোইনি may be caught only as জোই (yogi), and the source form with a first-use note keeps her distinct from Nairātmā.

proposals.definition: A word of uncertain sense in the first line of song 4: the thing the yoginī is asked to press. Its first part is probably ti-, 'three'. Munidatta cites it as tiyaṛa; the Tibetan translation has ka mgo, whose sense here is unclear.
proposals.symbolicImage: the tiaḍḍā that the yoginī is asked to press

symbolicReadings.referent: the three channels, lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtikā, which are pressed and made free of appearance

proposals.rationale: An obscure word that Munidatta reads as the three channels; keeping the source form (or at most 'the three') keeps his reading out of the line.

proposals.definition: An embrace (Sanskrit aṅkapālī; aṅka is 'lap' or 'flank'), which the poet asks the yoginī to give. Munidatta explains the word as if it were aṅka, 'mark', and pāl-, 'protect'. The Tibetan translation has yan lag 'khyud, 'embrace of the limbs'.
proposals.symbolicImage: the embrace the poet asks the yoginī to give

symbolicReadings.referent: she gives her own mark (aṅka, svacihna) to the practitioner and protects it (pālayati)
or else, through union marked by the moments beginning with vicitra, she gives the sequence of joys

proposals.rationale: Munidatta's reading rests on splitting the word, so the entry keeps 'embrace' in the line and his 'mark' in the notes.

proposals.definition: Evening (Sanskrit vikāla, Old Bengali biālī), the time the poet names for the rubbing of lotus and vajra. Munidatta takes the word as vi-kāla, 'without time'. The Tibetan translation gives both dus min, 'not the time', and dgongs mo, 'evening'.
proposals.symbolicImage: evening, the time named for the rubbing of lotus and vajra

symbolicReadings.referent: free of time (kālarahita): the yogi is told to realize directly the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, which is free of time

proposals.rationale: Munidatta reads the line through a pun on vikāla; the entry keeps 'evening' in the verse and his 'without time' in the notes.

proposals.definition: The juice or nectar (rasa) of the lotus, which the poet says he drinks after kissing the yoginī's mouth. The Tibetan translation has chu skyes khu ba, 'lotus juice'.
proposals.symbolicImage: the lotus nectar the poet drinks after kissing the yoginī's mouth

symbolicReadings.referent: ultimate (paramārtha) bodhicitta, described as the intoxicating honey of the uṣṇīṣa lotus

proposals.rationale: A compound image with its own reading in Munidatta; 'lotus nectar' reads naturally, with 'lotus juice' as the more literal variant.

proposals.definition: The protuberance on the crown of a buddha's head, one of the marks of a great being; tantric accounts of the body also use the word for the top of the head. Munidatta speaks of the honey of the uṣṇīṣa lotus (cp.04.m3).
proposals.rationale: A technical term in Munidatta's gloss on the lotus nectar that a reader will need explained; usually kept in source form in English.

proposals.definition: Ultimate: how things really are, as against the conventional level (saṃvṛti) at which they appear and are spoken of; the two together are the two truths. Munidatta speaks here of ultimate bodhicitta (cp.04.m3), where earlier songs have conventional bodhicitta.
proposals.rationale: The counterpart of the existing saṃvṛti ('conventional'); a fixed rendering keeps 'ultimate bodhicitta' and 'conventional bodhicitta' parallel.

proposals.definition: A code word of the twilight language. In the Hevajra verse Munidatta quotes, the fit (bhavya) is called 'great kāliñjara' and the unfit ḍiṇḍima (cp.04.m3); in his own sentence the Tibetan translation renders the word by its sense, skal ba dang ldan pa, 'fortunate'. As an ordinary name, Kāliñjara is a hill fort in central India.
proposals.symbolicImage: kāliñjara, in ordinary use the name of a hill fort

symbolicReadings.per: the Hevajra Tantra, as quoted by Munidatta

proposals.rationale: A twilight-language code word defined in the quoted Hevajra verse; kept in source form because the verse itself explains it.

proposals.definition: A code word of the twilight language. In the Hevajra verse Munidatta quotes, the unfit (abhavya) is called ḍiṇḍima and the fit 'great kāliñjara' (cp.04.m3). As an ordinary word a ḍiṇḍima is a kind of drum.
proposals.symbolicImage: ḍiṇḍima, in ordinary use a kind of drum

symbolicReadings.per: the Hevajra Tantra, as quoted by Munidatta

proposals.rationale: The partner of kāliñjara in the same verse; kept in source form for the same reason.

proposals.definition: The existence between death and the next birth, which many Buddhist schools say a being passes through before rebirth. In a scriptural verse Munidatta quotes, it is named with arising, abiding and ceasing, and all conceptual thought is called the work of wind and mind (cp.04.m3).
proposals.rationale: A doctrinal term in a quoted verse that a reader will need explained; 'existence' follows the Sanskrit bhava.

proposals.definition: Wind or breath; in tantric yoga, the vital winds (prāṇa) that move through the body's channels and carry the mind. Munidatta has the poet say that without the yoginī he cannot hold the vital wind, and quotes a verse calling all conceptual thought the work of wind and mind (cp.04.m3); Kāṇha's verse pairs mind and wind (cp.04.m5).
proposals.rationale: A core term of the tantric physiology Munidatta assumes, found three times in this unit under three words (prāṇavāta, vāyu, pavaṇa); one entry gives them one rendering.

proposals.definition: A word of uncertain sense in song 4: where the yoginī flows before reaching Oḍḍiyāna. Maṇi is 'jewel'; kula may be 'family' or, as elsewhere in the songs, kūla, 'bank'. The Tibetan translation has ma Ni kuN+Da li, perhaps from a different reading. Munidatta's paraphrase has the root of the jewel (maṇimūla) in its place.
proposals.symbolicImage: the maṇikula through which the yoginī flows

symbolicReadings.referent: the root of the jewel (maṇimūla), from which, having enjoyed the taste of play, she rises up and up to the wheel of great bliss (his paraphrase puts maṇimūla where the song has maṇikula; he gives no explicit gloss)

proposals.rationale: An obscure compound whose kula would otherwise be caught by the kula-shore entry; kept in source form until the reviewer chooses between 'jewel family' and 'jewel bank'.

proposals.definition: Oḍḍiyāna (also Uḍḍiyāna), a land celebrated in tantric Buddhism as a seat of yoginīs and a source of tantras, usually placed in the Swat valley in the northwest, though some locate it in Orissa. In song 4 the yoginī's course ends there; Munidatta's paraphrase has the wheel of great bliss in its place (cp.04.m4).
proposals.symbolicImage: Oḍḍiyāna, where the yoginī's course ends

symbolicReadings.referent: the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukhacakra), into which she is absorbed (his paraphrase puts it where the song has Oḍḍiyāna; he gives no explicit gloss)

proposals.rationale: A famous tantric place name, here in the vernacular form oṛiāṇa; English uses the standard Sanskrit form, as with Yamunā for jaunā.

proposals.definition: A husband's mother, in the joint household the figure of authority over a young wife. In song 4 key and lock are put in the mother-in-law's house. The Tibetan translation has sgyug mo, 'mother-in-law'.
proposals.symbolicImage: the mother-in-law's house, where key and lock are put

symbolicReadings.referent: the house of breath, the summit of Sumeru, to which the lord of yogis leads the avadhūtikā; his words śvāsam āgāraṃ ('breath', 'house') seem to echo sāsu gharem̐, and the Tibetan has dbugs kyi khyim, 'house of breath'

proposals.rationale: A household image whose reading rests on a sound-play (sāsu, śvāsa); the entry keeps the mother-in-law in the line.

proposals.definition: A key (Sanskrit kuñcikā, Old Bengali koñcā). In song 4 key and lock are put in the mother-in-law's house. The Tibetan translation has lde kyog, 'hooked key', both in the line and in Munidatta's comment.
proposals.symbolicImage: the key put, with the lock, in the mother-in-law's house

symbolicReadings.referent: with the lock: closing the lock, explained as blocking the door of the root of the jewel (maṇimūla)

proposals.rationale: Munidatta takes up the word by name (kuñcikā iti) and reads it; the entry keeps the key literal.

proposals.definition: A lock (compare Bengali tālā); the word tāla also means palm tree and musical time. In song 4 key and lock are put in the mother-in-law's house; in Kāṇha's verse quoted by Munidatta a firm lock is set at the door of the sky (cp.04.m5). The Tibetan translation of the line has lde mig, usually 'key'.
proposals.symbolicImage: the lock put, with the key, in the mother-in-law's house

symbolicReadings.referent: sealing the lock shut (tālasampuṭīkaraṇa), explained as blocking the door of the root of the jewel (maṇimūla)

proposals.rationale: Found in the song, in Munidatta's gloss and in Kāṇha's verse; the match form তাল is short and may catch other words (pātāla, tālu), and no Tibetan match is proposed because lde mig usually means key.

proposals.definition: A word the tantras use for the sexual union of yogic practice, usually spelled kunduru; in ordinary Sanskrit kunduru is olibanum, a fragrant resin. The poet calls himself a hero in kundura. Munidatta explains it as the imperishable bliss of uniting the two organs (cp.04.m6); the Tibetan translation keeps the word.
proposals.symbolicImage: kundura, in which the poet says he is a hero

symbolicReadings.referent: the union of the two organs (dvīndriyasamāpatti) and the imperishable bliss of that yoga, by which he crushes the enemy, the afflictions

proposals.rationale: A tantric code word that both Munidatta and the Tibetan translation treat as a term; kept in source form because its sense in the line is not plain.

proposals.definition: Hero; in the yoginī tantras also a title of the male adept, the partner of the yoginīs. The poet of song 4 calls himself a hero in kundura; Munidatta says he is one because he has crushed the enemy, the afflictions (cp.04.m6). The Tibetan translation of the line has no separate word for 'hero'.
proposals.rationale: A title with tantric weight that Munidatta explains; 'hero' is the plain rendering.

proposals.definition: A strip of cloth or rag (Sanskrit cīra), here raised like a flag: the poet says he has raised it among men and women. The Tibetan translation renders it rtags mtshan, 'sign, emblem'.
proposals.symbolicImage: the cloth the poet raises among men and women

symbolicReadings.referent: the mark of the lord of yogis (yogīndracihna), the eightfold mastery and the rest, raised to display the higher knowledges

forbiddenInLine: mark of the lord of yogis
proposals.rationale: The closing image of the song, which Munidatta reads as a mark of accomplishment; 'flag' keeps the image plain, though 'rag' or 'strip of cloth' is closer to cīra.

forms.translit: rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin
forms.lemma: rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin

proposals.definition: In Mahāyāna accounts of the path, the final meditative absorption, which like a vajra cuts through the last and subtlest obscurations just before awakening. Munidatta says Guḍḍarī speaks his own praise because he has directly realized it (cp.04.m6).
proposals.rationale: A technical term that recurs in Munidatta (the pañcakrama entry already mentions it for cp.01.m2); 'samādhi' follows the approved rendering of that entry.

proposals.definition: The eight powers that Indian yoga traditions ascribe to accomplished yogis, such as becoming minute, becoming light, and lordship over others. Munidatta names them as part of the mark of the lord of yogis that the poet raises (cp.04.m6); the Tibetan has 'the eight qualities, beginning with lordship'.
proposals.rationale: A technical list a reader of the commentary will need explained; in the manuscript the word is fused by sandhi with the one before it (…চিহ্নমষ্ট…), so the form is given resolved and the match form starts after aṣṭa-.

proposals.definition: The higher knowledges: extraordinary capacities that Buddhist texts ascribe to advanced practitioners, usually six (magical powers, the divine ear, knowing others' minds, recalling past lives, the divine eye, and the ending of the defilements). Munidatta says the poet raised his mark to display them (cp.04.m6).
proposals.rationale: A standard doctrinal term; in the manuscript it is fused by sandhi with the word before it (…মভিজ্ঞা…), so the form is given resolved and a second match form covers the fused spelling.

proposals.definition: Lacking intrinsic nature (svabhāva): the Madhyamaka teaching that nothing exists by its own nature, another way of stating emptiness. Munidatta opens his comment on song 4 by saying that Guṇḍarīpāda, through understanding the conduct of Heruka, teaches others that things are without intrinsic nature (cp.04.m1).
proposals.rationale: A key doctrinal term in the opening of the comment, to be kept distinct from the existing svarūpa ('true nature').

proposals.definition: In tantric yoga, one of the three main channels of the subtle body, usually described as running to the left of the central channel (avadhūtī). Munidatta names lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtikā as the three channels that are pressed and made free of appearance (cp.04.m2).
proposals.rationale: Named in the forbidden lists of existing entries (moon) but without an entry of its own; kept in source form, like avadhūtī.

proposals.definition: In tantric yoga, one of the three main channels of the subtle body, usually described as running to the right of the central channel (avadhūtī); the word also means 'tongue'. Munidatta names it with lalanā and avadhūtikā as the three channels that are pressed (cp.04.m2).
proposals.rationale: Named in the forbidden lists of existing entries (sun) but without an entry of its own; kept in source form, like avadhūtī.

proposals.definition: A channel of the subtle body. In tantric yoga the vital winds move through a network of channels, of which the chief three are lalanā, rasanā and the central avadhūtī. Munidatta speaks of pressing these three (cp.04.m2).
proposals.rationale: The general term behind lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtī; no Tibetan match form is proposed because rtsa also means 'root' (as in nor bu'i rtsa ba).

proposals.definition: 'Variety': in the Hevajra system, the first of the four moments (kṣaṇa) of yogic union, followed by vipāka, vimarda and vilakṣaṇa. Munidatta says the yoginī gives the sequence of joys through union with the characteristics beginning with vicitra (cp.04.m2).
proposals.rationale: Companion of the existing vilakṣaṇa entry; the match form বিচিত্র will also catch the ordinary adjective 'various', and sna tshogs is too common in the Tibetan to be a match form.

proposals.definition: A completion-stage practice of the Guhyasamāja tradition in which the breath is joined with the syllables oṃ āḥ hūṃ. Munidatta says that by its instruction the lord of yogis cuts off the grasping of the sides of moon and sun and makes firm the vajra of speech (cp.04.m5).
proposals.rationale: A technical practice whose phrase (vajrajāpopadeśena) already occurs once earlier in the text; the existing Nāgārjuna entry names it without an entry of its own.

proposals.definition: The mountain at the centre of the world in Indian cosmology, also called Meru; tantric texts also locate it within the body. Munidatta says the lord of yogis leads the avadhūtikā to the house of breath, the summit of Sumeru (cp.04.m5).
proposals.rationale: A cosmological name a reader will need explained; kept in source form.

proposals.definition: Meditation in which practitioners visualize themselves as the deity of a tantra, the foundation of tantric practice. Munidatta says the lord of yogis first makes firm the vajra of body, beginning with deity yoga (cp.04.m5).
proposals.rationale: A basic tantric technical term; 'deity yoga' is the usual English.

New source forms for an existing entry; nothing else in the entry is meant to change. The song and Munidatta use kamala for the lotus (kamala-kuliśa, 'lotus and vajra'), and the Tibetan has chu skyes; the entry so far lists only padma.

New source forms for an existing entry; nothing else in the entry is meant to change. kuliśa, 'vajra', stands on its own in the song's kamala-kuliśa and in Munidatta's gloss; the entry already treats kuliśa as a synonym (kuliśāravinda).

New source forms for an existing entry; nothing else in the entry is meant to change. A new spelling of the sun, suja (beside the entry's sūjja), in cāndasujabeṇi; the match form is short and could catch other words, so a longer one may be preferable.

New source forms for an existing entry; nothing else in the entry is meant to change. Munidatta's name for the yoginī of the song, nairātmayoginī (once nirātma-), which the Tibetan renders bdag med (ma'i) rnal 'byor ma; matching the whole compound stops it being read as nairātmya ('selflessness') plus a separate yoginī.

New source forms for an existing entry; nothing else in the entry is meant to change. Sandhi forms (-āvadhūtikā) that the listed অবধূতিকা cannot match, because the initial a- merges with the word before; the second form is given without the folio number that splits it in the manuscript (বির[৯]মানন্দাবধূতিকা).

New source forms for an existing entry; nothing else in the entry is meant to change. ambaru, 'sky', in Kāṇha's verse quoted in cp.04.m5 (the Tibetan has nam mkha'); tagged oben as a vernacular word, with the match also under san because the verse sits in a Sanskrit segment. Ambara can also mean 'garment'.

New source forms for an existing entry; nothing else in the entry is meant to change. A new spelling of the name, kahnu, in the signature line of his verse quoted in cp.04.m5 (the Tibetan has kAh+Na).

New source forms for an existing entry; nothing else in the entry is meant to change. sampradāya on its own, in Munidatta's 'yoginīs and yogins turned away from the lineage'; the shorter match form also covers the listed gurusampradāya and asampradāya.

New source forms for an existing entry; nothing else in the entry is meant to change. The Tibetan renders viramānanda as sna tshogs pa'i dga' ba, 'joy of variety', here and again in cp.04.m5 (sna tshogs pa dga' ba); recorded as an attestation only, with no match form, since it may reflect a different reading or system.

New source forms for an existing entry; nothing else in the entry is meant to change. tṛtīyapadena, 'with the third verse', introduces couplet 4 here, which confirms the count that leaves out the refrain; the token recurs in the text.

New source forms for an existing entry; nothing else in the entry is meant to change. nirābhāsīkṛtya, 'making free of appearance', said of the three channels; the prefix fuses with ābhāsa, so the listed forms would not catch it. The Tibetan reads differently here (shin du gsal snang du byas pa, 'made into very clear appearance').

questions: yoginī is proposed as keep-source-first-gloss ('yoginī'), although the existing 'yogi' entry is 'translate'. Please confirm.

tiaḍḍā is kept in source form, with 'the three' as a variant because ti- is probably 'three'. kamala-rasa is 'lotus nectar', with 'lotus juice' as the literal variant. cīrā is 'flag', though 'rag' or 'strip of cloth' is closer to cīra. Please choose.

maṇikula and Oḍḍiyāna: Munidatta does not gloss these words outright (no 'X iti Y'). His paraphrase of couplet 3 puts maṇimūla and mahāsukhacakra in their place. I have recorded these as his readings with that caveat; please decide whether that is enough to count as attested.
The last couplet spells the poet's name guḍarī. Should the bhaṇitā keep 'Guḍarī' or normalize to 'Guṇḍarī'? Both are listed as variants of Guṇḍarīpāda.

cp.04.m5 'sahajānandaikalolībhāvaṃ na śvāsam āgāraṃ': the 'na' probably belongs to an instrumental '-bhāvena'. The Tibetan has an instrumental (ro gcig pa'i ngo bos) and no negative. The sāsu reading rests on Munidatta's śvāsa … āgāra echoing sāsu ghara.

The Tibetan renders viramānanda as sna tshogs pa'i dga' ba ('joy of variety') in cp.04.m3 and cp.04.m5. I added it to that entry as an attestation without a match form; please decide whether the entry should also mention it.

Some match forms are short and may catch other words: তাল (lock; also in pātāla, tālu), সুজ (sun), বিচিত্র (vicitra; also the ordinary adjective), অম্বর (sky; also 'garment'), অরু (Aru), বীর (hero). Please narrow any that misfire.

Forms from Kāṇha's vernacular verse quoted inside Sanskrit segments (pavaṇa, tāla, ambaru, kahnu) are tagged oben. Their match forms are listed under both san and oben, because matching goes by the segment's language.

Not proposed: ধ্রু, the top candidate. It is covered by the dhruvapada definition, and a match form would tag every refrain cue. Also not proposed: 'mouth', although in cp.04.m3 Munidatta equates the yoginī's mouth with innate joy. Say if you want an entry for it.
Folio numbers inside words (শ্রীহেরুকচ[৮]র্য্যা in cp.04.m1, বির[৯]মানন্দ in cp.04.m5) stop the carya and viramānanda entries from matching there.
